body:
PIPELINE 319 FAILED — AND THE INJECTION WORKED. THE SAME TEST FAILED FOR A
DIFFERENT REASON, AND THE DIFFERENCE IS THE WHOLE RESULT.

    318 (dd1285fb63's predecessor, pre-injection):
        awaiting_notice_does_not_read_an_open_stdin_pipe ... FAILED
        "remained alive for 3.135800526s with an open stdin pipe"

    319 (post-injection, code identical to the current head):
        awaiting_notice_does_not_read_an_open_stdin_pipe ... FAILED
        "awaiting --notice exceeded its two-second budget: 2.008584508s"

THE PROCESS NO LONGER HANGS. It went from outliving the test at 3.14s to
COMPLETING at 2.0086s. The injection scoped exactly as I read it — the stdin
test still gets the 1s product bound and the process now exits promptly. MY
"one cmd.env, not a helper" VERIFICATION STANDS; the deadline is not leaking.

WHAT IS LEFT IS AN 8.6-MILLISECOND OVERSHOOT ON A 2-SECOND ASSERTION.
task_1283_protocol_cli.rs:345 asserts `elapsed < Duration::from_secs(2)` and
the run came in at 2.008584508s — 0.4% over, on a shared CI runner.

SO THE REMAINING FAILURE IS A TIGHT-BUDGET PROBLEM, NOT A DEADLINE PROBLEM,
and reporting it as "the same test failed again" would have sent someone back
to the injection — which is the thing that is now working.

AND IT IS THE SAME CLASS ONE LAYER OVER. The test carries its own hardcoded
timing constant: contract_budget = 2s, with reap_deadline = 3s and a comment
explaining the gap exists to avoid "a scheduler race exactly at the
assertion/kill boundary". The author already knew this boundary was raceable
and widened the REAP side while leaving the ASSERTION at a bare 2s. NOTICE_DEADLINE
was a magic timing constant that could not serve two callers; this is a magic
timing constant that cannot survive a loaded runner. Same family, and the fix
for the first one has just surfaced the second.

I AM NOT PROPOSING THE NUMBER. Widening 2s to 3s would be exactly the move you
refused on NOTICE_DEADLINE — moving a constant because a test failed, without
the argument. What the evidence supports is narrower: the assertion is
measuring WALL CLOCK ON A SHARED RUNNER against a bound with 8ms of headroom,
and the contract it claims to protect ("two-second budget") is a product
statement that deserves the same separate-the-test-from-the-product treatment
the deadline just got.

ONE CAVEAT I WILL NOT SMOOTH OVER: this is ONE observation at 2.0086s. It is
consistent with a marginal budget and it is also consistent with the command
being genuinely ~2s on that runner, in which case the budget is correct and
something else is slow. Distinguishing those needs more than one run — the
same denominator problem as STORY-1423's n=26.

#2019's verdict stands as CHANGES REQUESTED. The CI finding is now
RESOLVED-AND-FAILING-DIFFERENTLY rather than unresolved: the fix did what it
claimed, and it uncovered the next constant.

- claude-reviewer-1
